name: Brain Computer Interfaces
title: Brain Computer Interfaces
answer: Brain computer interfaces are systems that read neural activity and translate it into control signals for computers, prostheses, or communication devices, and sometimes write stimulation back into the nervous system. They span non invasive methods such as EEG, fNIRS, and MEG, and invasive methods such as electrocorticography and intracortical arrays. In the clinic, the field overlaps with neurorehabilitation, epilepsy monitoring, motor restoration, speech decoding, and sensory prosthetics. The site places this topic under Neuroinformatics and the Brain, part of The AI Physician, alongside its catalogue of 1000 medical AI models.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: BCI systems run on a chain of sensors, amplifiers, digitizers, and real time computing. Non invasive rigs rely on electrodes on the scalp, while implanted systems use electrode arrays, connectors, and sometimes wireless transmitters. The compute side includes low latency signal processing, embedded processors, and machine learning models for decoding. Clinical and research deployments also depend on data storage, synchronization hardware, and software for experiment control and neural data analysis. The site tracks 732 AI tools, and BCI work draws on general purpose signal processing and machine learning libraries.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work typically begins with a task design and a calibration session, where the system records neural signals while the user imagines or performs a movement, attends to a stimulus, or attempts speech. Signals are filtered, artifact removal is applied, and features are extracted in time, frequency, or spatial domains. A decoder, often a machine learning model, maps those features to commands, and the loop closes when the user sees or feels the result and adjusts. Iterative training, online adaptation, and validation against held out data are standard. The site tracks 800 scientific models, and BCI decoding draws on that wider modelling literature.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: BCI data are neural data, among the most sensitive categories, so consent, data minimization, and clear provenance from sensor to model matter. Implanted devices add surgical risk, device failure, cybersecurity exposure, and long term maintenance concerns. Regulatory pathways vary by jurisdiction and by whether the device is invasive, and the site tracks 215 compliance and regulation pages that cover such oversight. The site also tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows how claims can arise when AI enabled products cause harm. Researchers and clinicians must document data sources, model versions, and decision logs, and they must respect privacy rules and institutional review.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward higher channel counts, wireless implants, and longer term stability of electrodes. Decoding is shifting from simple motor commands to continuous speech, handwriting, and richer intent, with adaptive models that recalibrate over time. Non invasive systems are improving through better dry electrodes, wearable fNIRS, and transfer learning that reduces calibration burden. Clinical translation will depend on evidence from trials, reimbursement decisions, and standards for interoperability and security.
